extracted.intended_audience: readers or students of ancient philosophy (Plato's Gorgias)
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of the nature and moral value of rhetoric, flattery, power, punishment, and happiness within a Socratic dialogue (Plato's Gorgias). The text articulates standards for distinguishing true arts from sham practices and for judging what is truly good for the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art versus experience (criterion for an art)
rubrics_metrics.description: An art can explain and give reasons for the nature of its applications; mere experience (or routine) cannot. Socrates: 'An art I do not call it, but only an experience, because it is unable to explain or to give a reason of the nature of its own applications.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ability to explain/justify methods as the test: medicine is an art because it can account for why a treatment works; cookery is an experience because it aims at producing pleasure without giving reasons about true health. If a practice cannot state its rationale in terms of the true good of its domain, treat it as experience/sham, not art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric as counterfeit of politics / of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric is described as the 'ghost or counterfeit of a part of politics' — a branch of flattery that simulates justice while aiming only at persuasion and pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rhetoric by whether it pursues the soul's true good (justice) or merely produces conviction/pleasure. If it only imitates the forms of political speech without caring for justice, classify it as counterfeit/flattery rather than genuine political art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flattery's identifying features
rubrics_metrics.description: Flattery targets pleasure without regard for men's highest interests, deceives by simulating legitimate arts, and uses appearances (lines, colours, garments) to produce spurious results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label a practice 'flattery' when it (a) aims primarily at immediate pleasure or gratification, (b) cannot justify its ends in terms of the true good, and (c) deliberately simulates a higher art to deceive. Examples: cookery simulating medicine, tiring simulating gymnastic, sophistry simulating legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish apparent good from real good
rubrics_metrics.description: Appearances (e.g., apparent health) may differ from real goods; one must discern whether a condition is truly good or only seems good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the condition contributes to the genuine well‑being of the relevant subject (body or soul) rather than merely producing pleasurable appearances. Use expert/articulate standards (physician for body, judge/justice for soul) to detect real goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power is a good only if conducive to the possessor's true good
rubrics_metrics.description: Power (the capacity to do as one pleases) is not automatically a benefit; it is good only if the actions it enables conduce to the owner's real good. Doing as one thinks best can be an evil if done without sense (i.e., unjustly or foolishly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating power, ask whether the exercise of that power advances the possessor's moral/real well‑being (justice, wisdom) rather than merely enabling gratification or harmful acts. Examples: tyrants or rhetoricians who do as they please may lack true power if their acts are unjust and harm their souls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions are means to ends (intentionality test)
rubrics_metrics.description: People do things not for the sake of the intermediate actions themselves but for the further ends those actions serve (e.g., one drinks bitter medicine for health).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze motives by identifying the final end agents intend; this distinguishes superficial satisfaction (means) from the true desired good (end). Use this to critique rhetorical appeals that present means as ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doing injustice is worse than suffering injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates' claim that to do injustice is the greater evil than to suffer it — doing injustice harms the soul more than being harmed externally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge moral actions primarily by their effect on the actor's soul/character rather than by external consequences. Use logical argument (comparison of pain vs evil/hurtfulness; agent/patient relations) to substantiate which is worse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment (when just) benefits the punished soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Just punishment is described as honourable and good because it improves the soul and delivers one from the evil (injustice) of the soul: 'he who is punished is delivered from the evil of his soul.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing punishment, distinguish just corrective punishment (which cures vice and benefits the soul) from mere suffering or revenge. If punishment is performed according to the rule of justice and aimed at correction, it counts as a benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as the therapeutic art for the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice (the right exercise of judging and punishing) is the art that frees people from vice and injustice in the soul, analogous to medicine for the body and money-making for poverty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify practices that properly attend to the soul's good (education, law, just punishment) as genuine arts. Evaluate institutions (judges, laws) by whether they correct vice and restore the soul's health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty judged by pleasure and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty (of bodies, sounds, institutions, knowledge) is measured in terms of pleasure and usefulness: 'you would call them beautiful in reference to some standard... pleasure or utility or both.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating aesthetic or institutional goods, ask whether they produce pleasure, are useful, or both. This standard applies broadly (e.g., laws and institutions gain beauty insofar as they are useful/pleasant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for comparing evils: hurtfulness/disgrace/pain
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine which evil is greater, compare their hurtfulness, painfulness, or disgrace: the most disgraceful is the most hurtful or painful, and hence the greatest evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measures of pain, hurtfulness, and disgrace (especially to the soul) to rank evils. This reasoning underlies the claim that soul‑evils (injustice, intemperance) are the greatest evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of refutation: rhetorical plurality vs philosophical single-witness truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical 'refutation' often relies on many respected witnesses or popular opinion; philosophical refutation relies on a single rational witness (the interlocutor) and logical examination aimed at truth rather than numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating arguments, prefer reasoned refutation over appeals to majority respectability. Beware being 'sworn down' by a crowd; test claims by logical consistency and the one competent witness rather than aggregate prestige.
